why_how.text: Slippery roads reduce tire grip and lengthen stopping distance, so winter driving starts with knowing where ice hides.
Good tires and evenly adjusted brakes are what you rely on when grip is low.

scenario.text: Lu drives a four-wheel-drive truck on a clear road that crosses a shaded bridge after a cold night.

reasoning.text: Bridges and shaded spots can be icy when the rest of the road is clear, and four-wheel drive does not stop any sooner.

result.text: Lu slows before the bridge and leaves extra stopping room, even with four-wheel drive.

claim.text: Common mistake: believing four-wheel drive lets you stop sooner on ice.

correction.text: Four-wheel drive adds traction but not stopping power; it cannot stop any sooner than an ordinary car.

prompt.text: The highway is dry, but a shaded overpass lies ahead after a freezing night. What should you assume about it?

answer.text: It may be icy even though the rest of the road is clear.

rationale.text: Bridges, overpasses and shaded spots can stay icy when the surrounding pavement is not.

narration.text: This chapter gathers driving tips for winter, mountain roads, rural roads and work zones, and closes with defensive driving basics. We start with winter roads and how to prepare your vehicle for them. You will learn when snow and ice are most dangerous, which spots can stay icy when the rest of the road looks clear, what four-wheel drive can and cannot do, and what the handbook says about tire tread, chains, snow tires and brakes. These points shape every winter decision, from how fast you drive to how much space you leave ahead of you.

lines.text: Most dangerous as they begin to melt.

narration.text: Snow and ice are at their most dangerous as they begin to melt. Slippery roads reduce tire grip and lengthen stopping distance. So a sunny winter afternoon, when the surface starts to melt, can be more dangerous than a cold, frozen morning. Less grip means your tires have less ability to steer, speed up or slow down, and longer stopping distance means you need more room ahead to stop safely. Both effects point to the same habits you will see throughout this chapter: slow down, leave more space, and make every input gentle when the road could be slippery.

Overpasses, bridges, shaded spots and snow-packed stretches can be icy even when the rest of the pavement is clear. That means a road can look dry for miles and still hold icy patches in specific places. A bridge, an overpass, a curve shaded by a hill, or a stretch where snow has been packed down by traffic can all be slick while the pavement around them is not. When you see one of these places ahead in cold weather, slow down before you reach it, not once you are on it, and keep your steering and braking smooth across it.

Here are two linked traps. First, bridges, overpasses and shaded spots can stay icy when the surrounding pavement is not, so a clear road can still hold icy patches. Second, four-wheel drive improves traction but does not let a vehicle stop any sooner than an ordinary car. Four-wheel drive adds traction but not stopping power. A driver who trusts a clear road and a four-wheel-drive vehicle may arrive at an icy bridge too fast to stop. Questions often pair these ideas, so remember that neither a clear road nor four-wheel drive changes how long it takes to stop.

lines.text: Better, may be required, can still slip.

narration.text: Keep good tire tread. In winter, chains, snow tires or other traction devices are better than ordinary tires, and they may be required on highways. Even these can slip on slick pavement, so they are a help, not a guarantee. When a highway requires traction devices, it is because conditions are bad enough that ordinary tires are not enough. Having the right equipment ready before you leave lets you meet those requirements. But once you are driving, the same rules still apply: slow down, leave more following distance, and avoid sudden steering, braking or acceleration.

lines.text: Adjusted so every wheel brakes evenly.

narration.text: Keep brakes in good repair and adjusted so every wheel brakes evenly. On a slippery road, uneven brakes can pull the vehicle to one side or upset its balance just when grip is lowest. Even braking lets the car slow in a straight line, which gives you the best chance of staying in control. Brakes are one of the systems the earlier vehicle-checks lesson told you to have checked right away if they ever seem wrong. Winter is when that advice matters most, because a brake problem that feels minor on dry pavement can become serious on ice or packed snow.

Here is a quick check: after a freezing night, the highway is dry and sunny, but a shaded overpass lies just ahead. What should you assume about it, and does your four-wheel drive change your plan? Decide before reading on. Assume the overpass may be icy, because overpasses, bridges and shaded spots can be icy even when the rest of the pavement is clear. Four-wheel drive does not help you stop any sooner than an ordinary car; it only adds traction. So slow down before the overpass and keep extra stopping room. Slow before the ice, not on it.

lines.text: Four-wheel drive does not stop sooner.

narration.text: Let us review. Snow and ice are at their most dangerous as they begin to melt, and slippery roads reduce grip and lengthen stopping distance. Overpasses, bridges, shaded spots and snow-packed stretches can be icy when the rest of the pavement is clear. Four-wheel drive improves traction but does not stop any sooner than an ordinary car. Keep good tread; chains, snow tires or traction devices are better in winter and may be required, though they can still slip. Keep brakes in good repair and adjusted so every wheel brakes evenly. Next, skids and braking.

why_how.text: A skid means the tires have lost grip, so the first step is to stop adding gas or brake that keeps them sliding.
Anti-lock and non-anti-lock brakes need different techniques, so knowing your car's system matters.

scenario.text: Zoe's older car has no anti-lock brakes, and she must slow down on a slippery road.

reasoning.text: Without anti-lock brakes, use threshold braking, pressing the brake to just short of locking the wheels.

result.text: Zoe presses the brake firmly but stops short of lockup, keeping the wheels turning as the car slows.

claim.text: Common mistake: using the anti-lock braking technique on a car that has no anti-lock brakes.

correction.text: Threshold braking works on cars with or without anti-lock brakes, but anti-lock technique cannot be used without ABS.

prompt.text: A car without anti-lock brakes needs to slow on a slippery road. Which technique fits?

answer.text: Threshold braking, pressing the brake to just short of locking the wheels.

rationale.text: Threshold braking works with or without ABS, while the anti-lock technique needs ABS.

narration.text: Even careful drivers sometimes feel the tires slip on snow, ice or wet pavement. This lesson covers what to do when that happens. You will learn the general first response to a skid, how to handle a skid in a car with anti-lock brakes, what threshold braking is and when to use it, and which technique works on which kind of car. The instructions differ depending on your brakes, and practice questions test whether you can match each technique to the right situation. Knowing which system your own car has is part of being ready for winter.

lines.text: Lift off the gas and the brake together.

narration.text: When traction is lost or a skid begins, lift off the gas and the brake together, then steer the front wheels toward your intended path. Both feet come off together, and your hands do the work of pointing the front wheels along the path you want. This is the general starting point. The next slides explain how the response changes in a car with anti-lock brakes, and what to do in a car without them. Remember the order: lift off the gas and the brake together, then steer the front wheels toward your intended path. Hold that path calmly until the tires grip again, and resist any urge to stab at the pedals.

lines.text: Steer the way you want to go.

narration.text: With anti-lock brakes, if you begin to skid, ease off the gas, press the brake and steer the front wheels the way you want to go. So the anti-lock instructions include pressing the brake, while the general response begins with both feet off the pedals. If your car has anti-lock brakes, keep steady pressure on the brake pedal and keep steering toward your path rather than lifting off and on. In short: ease off the gas, press the brake, and steer the front wheels the way you want to go. Do not lift your foot off the brake and press it again; keep the pressure steady while you steer toward your path.

lines.text: Brake to just short of locking the wheels.

narration.text: Without anti-lock brakes, use threshold braking when skidding or on slippery roads. Threshold braking means pressing the brake to just short of locking the wheels. You press firmly, but stop before the wheels stop turning. Threshold braking works on cars with or without anti-lock brakes, but anti-lock braking technique cannot be used on a car without ABS. So threshold braking is the one technique that works on any car, while the anti-lock technique belongs only to cars that have anti-lock brakes. Find out which system your car has before winter arrives.

title.text: Match the technique to the car

lines.text: ABS: press the brake and steer.
Generic: both feet off, then steer.

narration.text: Here is the trap. The two skid instructions differ by brakes: with anti-lock brakes you ease off the gas and push on the brake while steering, and without them you use threshold braking just short of lockup. And a generic skid starts with both feet off the pedals, while an anti-lock skid adds pushing on the brake; in both, steer where you want to go. Questions mix these up, for example offering the anti-lock technique for a car without ABS. Ask first what kind of brakes the car has, then pick the matching technique, and always steer toward your intended path.

Here is a quick check: you are driving an older car that has no anti-lock brakes, and you need to slow down on a slippery road. Which braking technique fits, and could you use the anti-lock technique instead? Decide before reading on. Use threshold braking, pressing the brake to just short of locking the wheels. The anti-lock technique cannot be used on a car without ABS, while threshold braking works on cars with or without anti-lock brakes. If a skid begins, lift off the gas and steer toward your intended path. Know your brakes before winter.

lines.text: Feet off, steer where you want to go.

narration.text: Let us review. When traction is lost or a skid begins, lift off the gas and the brake together, then steer the front wheels toward your intended path. With anti-lock brakes, ease off the gas, press the brake and steer the way you want to go. Without anti-lock brakes, use threshold braking, pressing the brake to just short of locking the wheels. Threshold braking works on cars with or without ABS, but the anti-lock technique cannot be used without ABS. Next, winter visibility, snowplows and the space you need in snow.

why_how.text: You cannot react to what you cannot see, so every window must be cleared before a winter drive.
Plows and sanding trucks work slowly in bad conditions, so drivers must take extreme care around them.

scenario.text: Max comes up behind several government plows working in tandem across the highway with yellow lights flashing.

reasoning.text: Passing a government-operated plow working in tandem with other plows while its yellow lights flash is illegal.

result.text: Max stays back with an extra large gap and follows the plows until they finish.

claim.text: Common mistake: scraping only a small patch of the windshield for a short trip.

correction.text: Scrape off all ice, snow and frost even for a short trip, and keep defrosters and wipers working.

prompt.text: Plows are working side by side in tandem with yellow lights flashing. May you pass the government-operated one?

rationale.text: Be extremely careful around plows and sanding trucks, and never pass tandem government plows with flashing yellow lights.

narration.text: Snow and ice affect more than traction. They also block your view, bring slow-moving plows onto the road, and leave pedestrians and bicyclists struggling for footing. This lesson covers keeping your windows clear, how to behave around snowplows and sanding trucks, including when passing a plow is illegal, and how to space yourself from other vehicles and road users in snow and ice. Each rule is short, but together they make up much of what safe winter driving looks like on an ordinary snowy day in Colorado. Clear glass comes first.

lines.text: Scrape all ice, snow and frost.
Open a window for inside fogging.

narration.text: Keep defrosters and wipers working. Scrape off all ice, snow and frost, even for a short trip. And clear inside fogging quickly by opening a window. A small hole scraped in the windshield leaves you blind to the sides, where pedestrians, bicyclists and other cars may be. Short trips are not an exception, because a crash can happen in the first block as easily as the last. If fog builds up inside the glass while you drive, opening a window clears it quickly, so you do not have to drive with a blurred view. Clear all of it, every time.

lines.text: Be extremely careful behind or around them.

narration.text: Snow plows and sanding trucks flash yellow and blue warning lights, so be extremely careful as you come up behind or go around them. Use extra care near snowplows clearing snow with flashing yellow lights. Passing a government-operated plow working in tandem with other plows while its yellow lights flash is illegal. Plows often work together across several lanes, and trying to get past them puts you in the path of the snow they throw and the plows themselves. The road behind working plows is the road they have just cleared, so staying behind them is usually the better choice.

lines.text: Give walkers and riders extra room.

narration.text: In snow and ice, keep an extra large gap behind the vehicle ahead, slow down, and give pedestrians and bicyclists extra room to get around snow and ice. The larger gap matters because slippery roads lengthen stopping distance. Pedestrians and bicyclists may have to step or ride around snowbanks and icy patches, sometimes moving into the road to do it. Giving them extra room protects them if they slip. So in winter, every kind of space grows: the space ahead of you, the space beside walkers and riders, and the speed margin that lets you stop in time.

Here is a quick check: on a snowy highway you come up behind three government plows working side by side in tandem, with their yellow lights flashing. Traffic behind you is getting impatient. May you pass the plows? Decide before reading on. No. Passing a government-operated plow working in tandem with other plows while its yellow lights flash is illegal. Be extremely careful as you come up behind plows and sanding trucks, keep an extra large gap, and slow down. Your windows should already be fully cleared of ice, snow and frost.

Let us review. Keep defrosters and wipers working, scrape off all ice, snow and frost even for a short trip, and clear inside fogging quickly by opening a window. Snow plows and sanding trucks flash yellow and blue warning lights, so be extremely careful around them, and never pass a government-operated plow working in tandem with flashing yellow lights. In snow and ice, keep an extra large gap behind the vehicle ahead, slow down, and give pedestrians and bicyclists extra room. Next, mountain driving. Patience behind plows pays off.

why_how.text: Mountain roads combine steep grades, changing weather and hidden hazards, so speed control and caution matter more.
A struggling uphill vehicle should help others pass, while uphill traffic keeps the right of way.

scenario.text: Eli's loaded car slows to a crawl climbing a steep mountain road with cars lining up behind.

reasoning.text: Pull off at the first safe spot or keep right so others can pass; uphill vehicles have the right of way over downhill ones.

result.text: Eli keeps right and pulls off at the first safe turnout to let the line pass.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a downhill vehicle has the right of way on a mountain grade.

correction.text: On a mountain grade the uphill driver has the right of way, and a slow uphill vehicle keeps right or pulls off.

memory_support.text: Lower gear down, uphill goes first.

prompt.text: Going down a long, steep mountain grade, how should you keep your speed under control?

rationale.text: Mountain grades call for a lower gear going down, and uphill vehicles keep the right of way.

lines.text: Who goes first on a grade.

narration.text: Colorado's mountain roads are among the most beautiful in the country, and among the most demanding to drive. This lesson covers the hazards they bring, how to control your speed on steep grades, where passing is illegal, what you may find around mountain curves, and what to do when your vehicle struggles to climb. It also covers right of way on mountain grades. You met a related rule in the right-of-way chapter for narrow roads too tight for two vehicles; this lesson adds the general rule that uphill vehicles have the right of way over downhill ones.

lines.text: Lower gear going down steep grades.

narration.text: Mountain driving brings steep grades, changing weather, bicyclists, wildlife and rocks on the road. Shift to a lower gear to control speed going down steep grades. The handbook lists changing weather among mountain hazards, so be ready for conditions to differ from one stretch to the next. Rocks can fall onto the road, and wildlife and bicyclists may be around any curve. Keep your speed in a range where you could stop for any of them. Shift down before the descent begins, and watch for rocks, wildlife and bicyclists along the way.

lines.text: No passing near a crest or on a curve.
Or anywhere your view is blocked.

narration.text: Using the oncoming lane to pass is illegal near the crest of a hill, on a curve, or anywhere your view of oncoming traffic is blocked. Mountain roads are full of these places, so legal passing spots can be few. In the mountains, also expect intersections hidden by trees, brush or crops, and animals on or beside the road. A side road may appear suddenly from behind a stand of trees, and a deer may step out from the brush. Both are reasons to keep your speed moderate and your eyes moving, especially at dawn and dusk.

lines.text: Uphill vehicles have the right of way.
A slow climber keeps right or pulls off.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many drivers assume the downhill vehicle has priority because it is harder to stop. The handbook gives the opposite rule. On a mountain grade the uphill driver has the right of way, and a slow uphill vehicle should keep right or pull off to let others by. If your vehicle struggles up a steep road, pull off at the first safe spot or keep right so others can pass. Questions may describe a downhill driver refusing to wait for an uphill car and ask who was right. The uphill vehicle had the right of way.

Here is a quick check: you are about to start down a long, steep mountain grade. How should you keep your speed under control, and what hazards should you watch for? Decide before reading on. Shift to a lower gear to control your speed going down steep grades. Watch for changing weather, bicyclists, wildlife and rocks on the road, and expect intersections hidden by trees or brush. Remember that using the oncoming lane to pass is illegal near a hill crest, on a curve, or anywhere your view is blocked, and that uphill vehicles have the right of way.

lines.text: No passing where views are blocked.
Uphill has the right of way.

narration.text: Let us review. Mountain driving brings steep grades, changing weather, bicyclists, wildlife and rocks on the road, so shift to a lower gear to control speed going down steep grades. Using the oncoming lane to pass is illegal near the crest of a hill, on a curve or anywhere your view is blocked. Expect intersections hidden by trees, brush or crops, and animals on or beside the road. If your vehicle struggles uphill, pull off at the first safe spot or keep right; uphill vehicles have the right of way over downhill ones. Next, rural roads.

why_how.text: Rural highways have the highest death rate per mile driven of any road type, so their hazards deserve special attention.
Higher speeds on rural roads make passing bicyclists especially dangerous, which is why more room is needed.

scenario.text: Ivy drives a rural highway with narrow lanes and no shoulders and comes up behind a bicyclist.

reasoning.text: Many bicyclist deaths happen on rural roads because of higher speeds, so slow down and give more than the required three feet.

result.text: Ivy slows and waits until she can give the rider well over three feet before passing.

claim.text: Common mistake: assuming the quiet roads of the countryside are safer than city driving.

correction.text: Rural highways are the most dangerous roads, with the highest U.S. death rate per mile driven of any road type.

prompt.text: On a fast rural road, how much room should you give a bicyclist you are passing?

answer.text: More than the required three feet.

rationale.text: Higher rural speeds and wind blasts make riders vulnerable, so slow down and give more than three feet.

narration.text: Rural roads may feel calm and empty, but the handbook calls rural highways the most dangerous roads of all. This lesson explains why. You will learn the death-rate fact that makes rural highways stand out, the road features that make them risky, the hazards that can appear without warning, how rough and unpaved surfaces affect control, what potholes can do, and why bicyclists on rural roads need extra room. Knowing these hazards ahead of time helps you set a speed that leaves room for the unexpected, which is the main defense on any rural trip.

lines.text: Narrow lanes, no shoulders or guard rails.

narration.text: Rural highways are the most dangerous roads, with the highest U.S. death rate per mile driven of any road type. Rural roads may have sharp or blind curves, steep hills and dips, poor or hidden guide signs, narrow lanes that make passing hard, and no shoulders or guard rails. Each of these features leaves less room for error. A narrow lane with no shoulder means there is nowhere to go if you drift, and a blind curve means you may meet a hazard with little warning. Slower speeds give you the time and space those roads do not.

On rural roads, expect blind driveways, T-intersections and side streets hidden by plants. Expect rocks, debris and animals, farm vehicles crossing the road, unmarked railroad crossings, and slow or small vehicles like bicycles. Many of these hazards appear suddenly, from behind a crop field, a hedge or a hill. A slow farm vehicle may be just over the next rise. Scan far ahead and to the sides, and be ready to slow or stop. Watch the sides of the road as closely as the road itself, because farm vehicles, animals and small vehicles can appear without warning on rural routes.

lines.text: Rough or unpaved dirt and gravel.

narration.text: Rural pavement is often rough, or unpaved dirt and gravel with less traction. Washboarding on gravel roads can upset steering and control. Potholes can make the vehicle bounce or jolt and cause the tires to lose traction. On these surfaces, the same speed that feels comfortable on smooth pavement may be too fast. Less traction means longer stops and less steering grip, especially in curves. Slowing down on gravel and rough pavement, and watching ahead for potholes, keeps the tires in contact with the road and gives you more control when you need it.

title.text: A rider on a rural road

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you are on a fast two-lane rural highway with no shoulder, and you come up behind a bicyclist. How much room should you give the rider when you pass, and why? Decide before reading on. Give more than the required three feet, and slow down. Many bicyclist deaths happen on rural roads because of higher speeds, and dangerous wind blasts can lead to riders being struck. Remember that rural highways have the highest death rate per mile of any road type, and narrow lanes can make passing hard, so wait if you need to.

lines.text: More than three feet for riders.

narration.text: Let us review. Rural highways are the most dangerous roads, with the highest U.S. death rate per mile driven. They may have sharp or blind curves, steep hills and dips, hidden signs, narrow lanes and no shoulders or guard rails. Expect blind driveways, hidden intersections, debris, animals, farm vehicles, unmarked railroad crossings and slow vehicles. Rough and gravel surfaces have less traction, washboarding upsets steering, and potholes cost traction. Give bicyclists more than three feet on rural roads. Next, work zones.

why_how.text: Work zones change from day to day and put crews close to traffic, so drivers must stay alert and ready to stop.
Inattention causes most work-zone crashes, which is why fines are doubled and enforcement is added.

scenario.text: Pat drives through a construction zone where the posted limit is lowered and the car ahead suddenly slows.

reasoning.text: Obey work-zone speed signs and flaggers and watch the vehicle ahead, because most work-zone crashes are rear-end collisions caused by inattention.

result.text: Pat keeps to the lower limit, leaves space and stops smoothly behind the slowing car.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking most work-zone crashes involve hitting workers or equipment.

correction.text: Most work-zone crashes are rear-end collisions caused by inattention, and fines are doubled as in school zones.

prompt.text: What kind of crash is most common in work zones, and what causes it?

rationale.text: Work-zone fines are doubled as in school zones, and most work-zone crashes are rear-end collisions.

narration.text: Work zones change the rules of the road for a stretch. This lesson covers what work zones contain and how changes are announced, how to drive through them, what large projects may add, why crews are so exposed, how enforcement and fines change in work zones, and the kind of crash that happens most often there. You met work zones briefly in the speed chapter. Here you will see the full picture, including why simply paying attention is the single biggest safety step. Keep your attention on the vehicle ahead from the first warning sign to the last.

lines.text: Signs, cones and devices warn ahead.

narration.text: Work zones contain equipment and workers, and they may change routes daily. Signs, cones and other devices placed ahead warn of the changes. So a road you drove yesterday may follow a different path today, with lanes shifted or closed. The warning signs come before the work itself, giving you time to slow down and choose your lane. In a work zone, stay alert, be ready to stop suddenly, and never tailgate. Tailgating leaves no room to stop if the vehicle ahead brakes for a flagger, a lane shift or equipment entering the road.

lines.text: Reduced limits give time to react.

narration.text: Large projects may use flaggers, portable concrete barriers, complex signs and reduced speed limits. Those lower limits give drivers more time to read and react. Work-zone crews cannot be fully separated from traffic, and they must watch constantly for drivers who drift into the work area. That is a heavy burden to place on workers, which is why driver attention matters so much. Obey work-zone speed signs and flaggers. A flagger's directions take priority, just as an officer's would, so follow them even if the signal or sign seems to say something else.

lines.text: Fines doubled, as in school zones.

narration.text: Police enforcement is often added in work zones, and fines are doubled there as they are in school zones. The higher penalties reflect how exposed workers are and how often crashes happen in these areas. Watch the vehicle ahead, because most work-zone crashes are rear-end collisions caused by inattention. A driver who glances at a phone or looks at the work instead of the road can miss the car ahead slowing for a lane shift. In a work zone, keep your eyes on the traffic in front of you and leave enough space to stop smoothly.

Here is the trap. Many people picture work-zone crashes as cars hitting workers or equipment. The handbook says something different. Work-zone and school-zone fines are both doubled, and most work-zone crashes are rear-end collisions. Those rear-end crashes are caused by inattention. Questions may ask what kind of crash is most common in work zones and offer head-on or rollover crashes as tempting choices. The answer is rear-end collisions. The fix is the same habit taught in this lesson: watch the vehicle ahead, keep space, and never tailgate.

Here is a quick check: a friend says the biggest danger in a work zone is hitting the heavy equipment. What kind of crash does the handbook say is most common in work zones, and what causes it? Decide before reading on. Most work-zone crashes are rear-end collisions caused by inattention. So obey work-zone speed signs and flaggers, watch the vehicle ahead, stay alert, be ready to stop suddenly and never tailgate. Remember too that fines are doubled in work zones, as they are in school zones, and police enforcement is often added.

lines.text: Alert, ready to stop, no tailgating.

narration.text: Let us review. Work zones contain equipment and workers and may change routes daily, and signs, cones and other devices placed ahead warn of the changes. Stay alert, be ready to stop suddenly and never tailgate. Large projects may use flaggers, barriers, complex signs and reduced limits that give you more time to react. Crews cannot be fully separated from traffic. Enforcement is often added and fines are doubled, as in school zones. Most work-zone crashes are rear-end collisions caused by inattention. Next, defensive driving and phone laws.

why_how.text: You cannot count on others obeying every rule, so defensive driving and seat belts protect you from their mistakes.
Phone and texting laws limit distraction, with narrow exceptions for emergencies.

scenario.text: Dana wants to send a text while driving, using a hands-free accessory.

reasoning.text: Colorado bars texting while driving except to contact police or fire services or in an emergency; the texting exceptions do not include hands-free.

result.text: Dana waits until she is safely stopped and parked before texting.

claim.text: Common mistake: believing a hands-free accessory makes texting while driving legal.

correction.text: Hand-held phone use has a hands-free exception, but texting does not; both allow contacting police or fire and emergencies.

prompt.text: You have a hands-free system. Under Colorado law, may you use it to send a text while driving?

answer.text: No. The texting exceptions do not include a hands-free accessory.

rationale.text: Mobile device use has a hands-free exception, but texting does not.

narration.text: The last part of this chapter turns to defensive driving basics. This lesson covers why defensive driving matters, the seat belt rule for everyone in the vehicle, Colorado's laws on using a mobile device and on texting while driving, and how to hold and turn the steering wheel. The phone and texting laws look similar but have one important difference, and practice questions focus on it. By the end, you should be able to say exactly when phone use is allowed while driving, and why texting has a narrower set of exceptions.

lines.text: Others may not obey every rule.

narration.text: You cannot count on others obeying every rule, so drive calmly, ignore aggressive drivers and practice defensive driving. Defensive driving means expecting that someone may run a light, drift from their lane or stop suddenly, and keeping enough space and attention to respond. Ignoring aggressive drivers means not racing them, not blocking them and not reacting to their gestures. And make sure every person in the vehicle wears a seat belt. Seat belts protect you and your passengers in the crash you could not avoid, which is the last line of defense when everything else fails.

lines.text: Mobile device: police, fire, emergency, hands-free.

narration.text: Colorado law bars using a mobile device while driving except to contact police or fire services, in an emergency, or with a hands-free accessory. Colorado law also bars texting while driving except to contact police or fire services or in an emergency. The listed texting exceptions do not include a hands-free accessory. So a hands-free setup can make a phone call legal while driving, but it does not make texting legal. If you need to send a text, wait until you have stopped somewhere safe, unless you are contacting police or fire services or handling an emergency.

Here is the trap. Hand-held phone use has a hands-free exception, but texting does not; both allow contacting police or fire and emergencies. Many drivers assume that if hands-free makes calls legal, it must make texts legal too. It does not. Questions may describe a driver dictating a text through a hands-free system and ask whether that is allowed. Under the texting law's exceptions, hands-free is not listed. Keep the two laws separate: a hands-free call can be legal, while a text is legal only for police, fire or an emergency.

lines.text: Hands at eight and four or nine and three.

narration.text: Keep both hands on the wheel at eight and four or nine and three o'clock. Turn with the hand-over-hand or push-pull-slide method. Never palm the wheel, and never let it slide through your fingers after a turn. These positions match what you learned in the basic driving chapter. Letting the wheel slide back on its own after a turn means you are not fully in control of where the car goes in those moments. Guiding the wheel back with your hands keeps the car on the path you choose, which is the heart of defensive control.

Here is a quick check: your car has a hands-free system, and you want to dictate and send a text message while driving. It is not an emergency, and you are not contacting police or fire services. Is that legal in Colorado? Decide before reading on. No. Colorado bars texting while driving except to contact police or fire services or in an emergency, and those texting exceptions do not include a hands-free accessory. A hands-free phone call, by contrast, is within the mobile device law's exceptions. Wait until you are safely stopped to text.

Let us review. You cannot count on others obeying every rule, so drive calmly, ignore aggressive drivers and practice defensive driving. Make sure every person in the vehicle wears a seat belt. Colorado bars mobile device use while driving except for police or fire, emergencies, or with a hands-free accessory, and bars texting except for police or fire or emergencies, with no hands-free exception. Keep both hands on the wheel at eight and four or nine and three, turn hand-over-hand or push-pull-slide, and never palm the wheel. Next, scanning and following distance.

why_how.text: Looking far ahead prevents last-second braking or swerving, because you see trouble early.
Regular mirror checks and a three-second gap keep you aware of traffic behind and ahead.

scenario.text: Lee follows a car on a highway and wants to check whether the gap is safe.

reasoning.text: When the car ahead passes a fixed point, count three seconds; if you reach the point first, you are following too closely.

result.text: Lee counts, reaches the sign at two seconds, and eases off until the gap reaches three seconds.

claim.text: Common mistake: mixing up the times for looking ahead, mirror checks and following distance.

correction.text: Look ten seconds ahead, check the mirror every five to eight seconds, and leave three seconds behind the car ahead.

memory_support.text: Ten ahead, mirror often, three behind.

prompt.text: You count from a fixed point and pass it at two seconds behind the car ahead. What does that tell you?

rationale.text: Under normal conditions you should reach the point no sooner than three seconds after the car ahead.

narration.text: This final lesson of the chapter is about where your eyes go and how much space you keep. You will learn how to scan around you and at intersections, how far ahead to look, how often to check your rearview mirror, and how to use the three-second rule to judge your following distance. Each habit comes with a time, and the three times are different, which makes them easy to mix up. We will tie each number to its job so you can keep them straight, both on the test and on the road. Keep the three times tied to their jobs.

lines.text: Scan ahead, to the sides, behind.
Left, right and left again at intersections.

narration.text: Scan ahead, to the sides and behind. Always look left, right and left again when turning at, crossing or entering an intersection, watching for pedestrians, bicyclists and motorcyclists. The second look to the left catches anything that appeared while you were looking right. Pedestrians, bicyclists and motorcyclists are smaller and easier to miss, so look specifically for them rather than only for cars. This scanning habit matches what you learned for the drive test, and it applies on every trip. Look for walkers, riders and motorcyclists every time.

lines.text: Look at least ten seconds ahead.
About a block in the city, half a mile open road.
Mirror every five to eight seconds.

narration.text: Look at least ten seconds down the road, about one block in the city or half a mile on the open road, to avoid last-second braking or swerving. Check your rearview mirror every five to eight seconds, more often in heavy traffic, and especially when changing lanes, slowing, backing, leaving an intersection or going down a long or steep hill. Looking far ahead lets you spot problems early, while regular mirror checks tell you what is behind you before you need to act. Together they keep you aware of the whole space around your vehicle, not just the bumper ahead.

lines.text: Car ahead passes a fixed point.

narration.text: Under normal conditions, use the three-second rule. When the car ahead passes a fixed point, such as a sign or a pole, count three seconds. If you reach the point before you finish counting, you are following too closely. Then ease off until you can count to three. The rule works at any speed, because it measures time, not distance. Remember that it is for normal conditions. In bad weather, at night or in snow and ice, earlier lessons told you to leave more following distance, so treat three seconds as a minimum when the road is good.

lines.text: Five to eight seconds: mirror checks.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Three different times guide your eyes and spacing: look ten seconds ahead, check the mirror every five to eight seconds, and leave three seconds behind the car ahead. Questions often swap them, offering three seconds for looking ahead or ten seconds for following distance. Tie each number to its job. The largest time, ten seconds, is how far ahead your eyes reach. The middle range, five to eight seconds, is how often you glance behind. The smallest, three seconds, is the minimum gap to the car ahead in normal conditions.

lines.text: You pass the sign at two seconds.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: on a dry highway, the car ahead passes a sign, and you start counting. You reach the same sign at the count of two. What does that tell you, and what should you do? Decide before reading on. You are following too closely, because under normal conditions you should reach the point no sooner than three seconds after the car ahead. Ease off until you can count to three. Keep your other habits going too: look at least ten seconds ahead, and check your rearview mirror every five to eight seconds. Three seconds is the minimum.

lines.text: Ten seconds ahead; mirror every five to eight.
